masthead_title: The whole curve flags higher for a second straight day, and it's dragging duration-sensitive software down with it
regime_line: Every Treasury tenor this system tracks is flagged for a second consecutive session (10-year z +2.06, the largest move on the board), and Tuesday's selloff spread beyond bonds into the most rate-sensitive corner of the stock market — high-multiple software — while California's utilities staged a partial, catalyst-free bounce and oil extended its Iran-driven climb.
provenance_note: Stated reasons and press framing via web search with named-source attribution (the standing source): CNBC, Benzinga, Bloomberg, TechTimes, The Motley Fool, Investing.com, Yahoo Finance, 24/7 Wall St., AlphaStreet, MarketBeat. No paid services used.
claims_section_html:
Claims ledger — one confirmed, two still open

One claim came due today and grades cleanly; two others remain live and are updated below before any new narrative is written (§4B).

  • CL-0005 — confirmed. Opened 08-26: did the pre-earnings semis rally (AMD, Marvell, Cadence, Lumentum, Coherent) reflect durable AI-capex conviction rather than positioning that unwinds, tested by whether SMH's cumulative return versus SPY since the 08-25 close stayed no worse than −2 percentage points, through today. Through Tuesday's close (the most recent available), SMH is down 1.91% since the baseline against SPY's 0.54% decline — a −1.37pp relative gap, comfortably inside the −2pp floor that would have refuted it. Confirmed — though the irony is that today's own semis-adjacent selloff (see Movers, below) is what's eating into that cushion; had this claim graded a week from now instead of today, the answer might read differently.
  • CL-0007 — still open (due 2026-09-03, one trading day left, grades against that specific day's close). Directionally supportive and strengthening: this system's own WTI series closed Tuesday at $90.22, up 5.2% on the day and well clear of the $85 line the claim will test tomorrow — this morning's reporting (Bloomberg) describes further U.S.-Iran strikes near the Strait of Hormuz overnight, with Brent trading above $95.
  • CL-0008 — still open (due 2026-09-09). Edison International and PG&E both bounced Tuesday (EIX +8.93%, PCG +5.95%) — see Movers below — but this system's IG OAS reading (dated Friday 08-28, one-day lag as usual) is unchanged at 0.80%, still inside the +5bp band the claim allows. No sign yet of the wildfire-liability shock spreading into broader investment-grade credit, but the test window runs another five trading days.

A new conditional claim opened this morning: CL-0009 — Tuesday's broad software/cybersecurity selloff (CrowdStrike, Palo Alto Networks, Datadog, Fortinet, Oracle, Cadence and others, each down 5-8%) is being driven by the Treasury-yield repricing rather than sector-specific demand concerns, tested by whether this system's own UST 10Y series stays at or above 4.70% (within 9bp of today's 4.79% close) while SMH's cumulative return vs. SPY worsens by at least 1 additional percentage point from today's level — both would need to hold together to confirm a persistent rate/software link; 10Y falling back below 4.70% while software recovers relative to SPY would refute it — through 2026-09-09.
story_html:
This morning's press narrative runs on two tracks that turn out to be the same story told twice. First, rates: CNBC and TechTimes both frame Tuesday as the day fed-funds-futures odds of a quarter-point September hike jumped to roughly 68%, up from about 40% a week ago, as the market keeps re-pricing Fed Chair Warsh's hawkish Jackson Hole tone from Friday. Second, and downstream of the first: Benzinga's markets desk describes Tuesday's slide in high-multiple software names — CrowdStrike, Palo Alto Networks, Datadog among them — as "rising Treasury yields... crushed high-multiple software stocks, not any fundamental weakness," with the 10-year's push toward 4.8% cited directly as the mechanism. Layered on top, Bloomberg reports fresh U.S. strikes on Iranian targets near the Strait of Hormuz overnight, with crossings through the strait reportedly down sharply from a week ago — the reason oil is up again this morning.

Does the state file confirm the rates story? Yes, more clearly than at any point this cycle. All four Treasury tenors this system tracks are flagged together for a second straight session, and the 10-year is today's largest single flag (z +2.06 — higher than all but a handful of days in the past six months) with the 2-year, 30-year, and 3-month right behind it (z +1.91, +1.93, +1.66). SOFR, the overnight funding rate that anchors floating-rate loans, is flagged too (z +1.51), and the 3-month/10-year spread — a classic recession-risk gauge — widened to a level this system also flags (z +1.56), which on its own would normally read as growth optimism re-pricing rather than stress; paired with everything else here it reads as "the whole curve moved up together," not a shape change. Does it confirm the software story? The correlation, at least: Tuesday's software decline (see Movers, below) landed on the same day the 10-year pushed to its highest level in this system's history, and Benzinga's reporting attributes the move directly to that mechanism. This brief treats "rates are driving the software selloff" as a hypothesis rather than a settled fact — it's logged as a new claim (CL-0009, below) rather than adopted into this brief's own voice. Credit, meanwhile, stayed calm — high-yield spreads actually tightened a touch (2.63%, z −1.10, near a six-month low) and investment-grade spreads barely budged (0.80%, z +0.20) — which is the detail that keeps today's tag at "tightening" rather than "stress": rates are repricing hard, but nothing in the credit market says anyone doubts anyone's ability to pay.
dashboard_lag_note: Observation dates in parentheses where they trail the 2026-09-01 market close: the TIPS real yield, breakeven, both credit-spread series, and SOFR publish a day behind (§5), dated to Monday 08-31; Fed balance sheet and TGA are the weekly Thursday H.4.1 release, dated to Wednesday 08-26. Flagged rows (⚑): far outside the past-6-months normal range — see the Reading key below.
dashboard_interp_html: Tuesday added another leg to Friday's move rather than reversing it: the 10-year rose another 4 basis points to 4.79%, the 2-year rose 5bp to 4.39%, and the 30-year and 3-month both added a couple of basis points too — small daily moves that matter because they're stacking on top of an already-elevated base, which is why all four are flagged together for the second day running. In real terms: anyone with an adjustable-rate mortgage reset coming up, a money-market fund, or a CD renewing soon is now pricing off a genuinely higher curve than existed two weeks ago, not a one-day scare. Using Monday's fully-published data (the most recent day with every piece available, one day behind Tuesday's close): the real yield (what investors demand after inflation — mostly a growth-and-Fed-policy number) sits at 2.44%, up another 2bp, while the breakeven (the market's implied inflation rate) was flat at 2.31% — the same pattern this brief has now shown two days running, where the move is coming from the real-rate side, not an inflation scare. SOFR (the overnight rate that floating-rate loans and money funds anchor to) rose 3bp to 3.68% and is itself now flagged (z +1.51) for the first time this cycle. Credit stayed the exception to all of this: high-yield spreads (2.63%, dated Monday) actually improved slightly and sit near a six-month low (z −1.10), and investment-grade spreads (0.80%) are barely moved (z +0.20) — a genuine, quiet positive that keeps this reading a rates story rather than a credit-quality scare. The overnight reverse repo facility (where money funds park spare cash overnight) fell back to $0.72B from Monday's month-end spike to $6.73B, confirming that jump was calendar plumbing as flagged yesterday, not a liquidity shift. Fed balance sheet and Treasury cash balance remain "thin history" series (§4) — directional only, no z-score confidence yet.
movers_html:
How this section works: all 503 S&P constituents scanned mechanically; a stock qualifies only by moving >4% (>2.5% for the 50 biggest) — never by seeming interesting. 45 name candidates and 1 sector divergence qualified Tuesday; cap is 3 names + a sector note.

CRWD −6.90% (215.07, from 231.00) — what happened: CrowdStrike's sharpest one-day drop in weeks, part of a broad decline across high-multiple software and cybersecurity names (Palo Alto Networks −5.24%, Datadog −5.57%, Fortinet −5.31%, Oracle −5.23%, Ciena −5.87% also qualified this system's mechanical screen). Stated reason: Benzinga's markets desk attributes the slide directly to Tuesday's Treasury selloff — "rising Treasury yields... crushed high-multiple software stocks, not any fundamental weakness" — noting CrowdStrike had entered the session up 97% year-to-date, one of the sharpest large-cap tech gains of 2026, which set up an outsized reaction to the rate move. Why it matters: the cleanest, most direct read-through in today's brief — this is the equity-market transmission of the very Treasury-curve story leading the dashboard above, not a separate narrative. Six-plus names clearing the mechanical 4% screen in the same sub-sector on the same day is breadth, not noise.

CDNS −7.60% (313.04, from 338.78) — what happened: Cadence Design Systems' worst day in months, alongside a smaller decline in peer Synopsys. Stated reason: Synopsys (a direct competitor in chip-design software) reported quarterly results that beat on both revenue and earnings and raised full-year guidance, but flagged what Investing.com and AlphaStreet describe as "muted backlog support" alongside the beat — reporting says investors read that as a read-across warning for the whole chip-design-tool industry, not company-specific noise, and sold Cadence on it even though Cadence itself reported nothing today. Why it matters: chip-design software sits directly upstream of the AI capex cycle this brief tracks at the cycle level (§8 wall applies — no view offered on any specific name's investment merit): a "muted backlog" comment from one of the two dominant EDA vendors is exactly the kind of early demand-signal this brief's Tier 3 section exists to catch, worth watching for confirmation in the weeks ahead rather than treating as settled today.

EIX +8.93% (58.80, from 53.98) — what happened: Edison International's sharpest one-day gain in years, with PG&E also up 5.95% (14.06, from 13.27) in the same move, one day after both posted some of their worst single-day declines in decades (Monday's wildfire-liability selloff, covered in this brief's 09-01 edition). Stated reason: reporting found no fresh legislative or regulatory catalyst behind Tuesday's bounce — coverage characterizes it as investors reassessing valuation after Monday's severe, arguably overdone decline, not a reversal of the underlying wildfire-liability news. Why it matters: a partial, catalyst-free technical bounce rather than a resolution of the story CL-0008 is tracking; nothing here changes the reconciliation above, and this brief will keep watching whether it holds.

Sector note: Energy (XLE) beat the S&P 500 by 1.95 percentage points Tuesday (+1.27% vs. −0.69%), the only sector divergence to clear this system's mechanical 1.5pp threshold — consistent with WTI's 5.2% jump on the Iran/Strait-of-Hormuz escalation covered above and in the open CL-0007 claim.
chart_of_day_why: Largest |z| flag on the entire board today is the 10-year Treasury yield (z +2.06), edging out the 30-year (+1.93) and 2-year (+1.91) — and it's the series directly behind both of today's dashboard and movers stories: the curve's second straight flagged session, and the discount-rate mechanism behind the software selloff covered in Movers.
tier3_html:
Daily read: semis (SMH) fell 2.09% Tuesday against the S&P 500's 0.71% decline, pulling CL-0005's cumulative read (SMH vs. SPY since the 08-25 baseline) to −1.37pp — the claim itself still confirmed as of today's grading (see Claims, above), but the trend is now moving the wrong direction into a week where duration-sensitive names are broadly under pressure. Separately, Cadence Design Systems fell 7.60% on a chip-design-software peer's "muted backlog" guidance comment (see Movers) — a name worth watching as an early demand signal for the AI capex cycle, not yet a confirmed one.

Financing watch: no new dated news on hyperscaler issuance or vendor-financing structures surfaced in this morning's search. The rates backdrop is the relevant structural note today: with the long end of the Treasury curve at cycle highs (30Y at 5.27%), any AI-adjacent debt issuance priced this week prices off a meaningfully higher risk-free base than it would have a month ago — a mechanism worth remembering even without a specific issuance data point today.
calendar_note_html: Today's most relevant release is ADP private payrolls at 8:15am ET (forecast 47K, previous 44K, medium impact) — a preview of Friday's official nonfarm payrolls report and a direct input to the Fed's dual mandate: a soft print would complicate this week's hawkish rate-hike repricing by suggesting the labor side of the economy is cooling even as the Fed leans tougher on inflation, while an in-line-or-better number would reinforce today's story that the economy can bear a September hike. The Fed's Beige Book (2:00pm ET, the central bank's own qualitative read on regional economic conditions ahead of the September 16 decision) is worth a skim for language on hiring and pricing power, even though this system doesn't score it numerically. Factory Orders (10:00am, low impact) and weekly Crude Oil Inventories (10:30am, low impact but relevant given today's oil story) round out the morning.
concept_unit: Unit 2 · Real vs. nominal decomposition · segment 3 of roughly 6
concept_title: The real yield has two pieces too: expected path and real term premium
concept_html: The last two segments split the nominal 10-year yield into a real yield (TIPS) and a breakeven (implied inflation). Today, go one layer deeper: the real yield itself splits into two pieces — the expected path of real short-term rates (roughly, how tight the Fed will keep policy after backing out inflation) and the real term premium (the extra compensation investors demand for the risk and uncertainty of holding a 10-year bond instead of rolling over short-term ones). This matters for reading today's move specifically: the real yield has now risen for two straight sessions (2.42% Friday → 2.44% Monday, the most recent published pair) alongside rising fed-hike odds reported this morning (roughly 68%, up from 40% a week ago per CNBC/TechTimes) — that combination points toward the expected-path piece doing the work, not the term-premium piece, because a genuine path repricing is exactly what should happen when the market moves the odds of an actual Fed decision. This system can't yet decompose real yields into path versus premium numerically (that requires a term-structure model beyond what this system computes), so today's read is qualitative, not a script-verified split like the real/breakeven decomposition — flagged here as a limit of what this brief can currently prove, not a claim it's making with confidence.
client_translation: "Even the 'real' part of a bond yield has two pieces — how tight the Fed will actually be, and how much extra investors want for the uncertainty of a ten-year commitment — and right now the moves line up with the market believing the Fed, not just getting nervous about holding long bonds."
client_lens_html:
• "Why did my tech-heavy fund drop so much yesterday when the S&P was only down a little?" — Rising Treasury yields hit high-multiple software and cybersecurity stocks (CrowdStrike, Palo Alto, Datadog, Oracle among them) disproportionately, because their value depends more on far-future earnings, which a higher discount rate shrinks more (see Movers, above). A useful, concrete illustration of duration risk — not just in bonds, but in growth stocks too.
  • "Is the Fed really going to hike in September?" — Reporting this morning puts the market-implied odds around 68%, up sharply from about 40% a week ago (CNBC, TechTimes). This system's own data confirms the direction — the whole Treasury curve is now flagged higher for a second straight day — but the actual decision isn't until September 16, and today's ADP payrolls print (8:15am) is one of the next real inputs to that debate.
  • "Did Edison and PG&E recover?" — Partially: both bounced 6-9% Tuesday after Monday's historic declines, but reporting found no new catalyst behind the bounce — it reads as a reassessment of Monday's selloff rather than a resolution of the underlying wildfire-liability story this brief is still tracking (CL-0008, due 09-09).
